pos: v. (third person singular present of say; rendering Hebrew 'amar and ne'um, Greek legei)
etymology: From Saxon sægþ, the third person singular present of secgan, to say. It is the older says, and in the Authorized Version it is above all the verb of the prophetic formula — Thus saith the LORD — which occurs some four hundred times.
biblical_def: Saith is the third person singular present of say, and its great office in Scripture is the messenger formula of the prophets. Thus saith the LORD is not a preface the prophet chose; it is the credential of a herald who carries another man's words and may not alter them. Jeremiah uses it to contradict the whole national mood: “Thus saith the LORD; Deceive not yourselves, saying, The Chaldeans shall surely depart from us: for they shall not depart” (Jeremiah 37:9). Ezekiel uses it to pronounce a sentence no man would invent (Ezekiel 35:14). And at the summit of the Abrahamic covenant the LORD swears by Himself with the same verb: “By myself have I sworn, saith the LORD” (Genesis 22:16). The present tense matters. The prophets do not say the LORD said, as though reporting an old communication, but saith — the word is being spoken now, and the hearer stands under it now. The Gospels use the same form for Christ's living speech: “he saith unto them, Our friend Lazarus sleepeth” (John 11:11). Scripture is not a record of what God once said; it is what God says.
webster_summary: The third person singular of the present tense of say; the older form of says. In Scripture it is the verb of the prophetic messenger formula, Thus saith the LORD, and of Christ's own living speech in the Gospels.
webster_full: SAITH, v. [Sax. sægþ.] The third person singular of the present tense of say; contracted in modern usage to says.
2. To speak; to utter in words; to declare.
3. In the prophetic writings it introduces the words of God delivered by a messenger; as, Thus saith the LORD.
4. It is retained in the solemn style and throughout the common version of the Scriptures.
5. In Scripture, By myself have I sworn, saith the LORD, Gen. 22; Thus saith the LORD; Deceive not yourselves, Jer. 37.
corruption_summary: The formula Thus saith the LORD is claimed today by men who have received no such word — the modern prophet, the impression taken for revelation, the leader who baptises his own preference in the language of Sinai. The canon is closed, and the formula belongs to Scripture.
corruption_paragraphs: The New Apostolic Reformation and the wider charismatic prophecy movement have restored the formula without restoring its terms. In Scripture a prophet who spoke presumptuously in the LORD's name was to die, and the test was absolute accuracy; no allowance was made for a word that was mostly right or right in spirit. Modern prophetic ministry regularly fails at precisely this point and then rewrites the failed word as a misheard impression, which is an admission that the formula was never warranted. The dictionary's position is the cessationist one held across the Reformed tradition: the canon is complete, and God now speaks to His church by His written word, illuminated by His Spirit.

A quieter version of the same abuse is more common and does more damage, because it wears no supernatural claim. It is the preacher, the counsellor, or the parent who attaches divine authority to his own judgment — announcing as God's will what Scripture nowhere says. The remedy is the discipline the formula itself implies: a herald may say thus saith only of what he was actually given. Where Scripture has spoken, speak with all boldness and without apology; where it has not, say so plainly and reason as a fallible man among fallible men.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'amar is the ordinary verb of saying, and koh 'amar YHWH is the messenger formula; ne'um YHWH, rendered saith the LORD, is the oracle marker; Greek uses legei, the present of lego.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'amar (H559) — to say, to speak, to command; the verb of the formula koh 'amar YHWH, thus saith the LORD.
Hebrew ne'um (H5002) — an utterance or oracle; rendered saith the LORD, marking the words as God's own.
Hebrew dabar (H1697) — a word, a matter, a thing; that which the prophet is given to carry.
Greek legei (G3004) — he saith; the present indicative, used for Christ's living speech in the Gospels.
Saxon sægþ — the Old English third singular present of secgan, to say.
usage: Of the LORD swearing by Himself in covenant: By myself have I sworn, saith the LORD (Genesis 22:16).
Of a prophet contradicting the national mood: Thus saith the LORD; Deceive not yourselves (Jeremiah 37:9).
Of Christ's living speech to His disciples: he saith unto them, Our friend Lazarus sleepeth (John 11:11).
scriptures: Genesis 22:16
And said, By myself have I sworn, saith the LORD, for because thou hast done this thing, and hast not withheld thy son, thine only son:
Jeremiah 37:9
Thus saith the LORD; Deceive not yourselves, saying, The Chaldeans shall surely depart from us: for they shall not depart.
Ezekiel 35:14
Thus saith the Lord GOD; When the whole earth rejoiceth, I will make thee desolate.
John 11:11
These things said he: and after that he saith unto them, Our friend Lazarus sleepeth; but I go, that I may awake him out of sleep.

pos: v. (third person singular present of come; rendering Hebrew participles, Greek erchetai)
etymology: From Saxon cymþ, the third person singular present of cuman, to come. In the Authorized Version it frequently renders a Greek present used of the future — the prophetic present, in which what is certain is spoken of as already on its way.
biblical_def: Cometh is the older comes, and in Scripture it carries a distinctive weight: the present tense used of what is certainly approaching. “in such an hour as ye think not the Son of man cometh” (Matthew 24:44) does not merely predict the second advent; the present tense puts it already in motion, and the exhortation be ye also ready follows from that. The palm-branch crowd greets the King with the same participle: “Blessed is the King of Israel that cometh in the name of the Lord” (John 12:13), citing the psalm of the coming one. It is equally the verb of quiet dependence: “Truly my soul waiteth upon God: from him cometh my salvation” (Psalm 62:1) — salvation described not as a thing achieved but as a thing arriving from outside. And in the parable of the lost sheep, the shepherd's return is the hinge of the joy: “when he cometh home, he calleth together his friends and neighbours” (Luke 15:6). Whether of Christ's advent, of salvation, or of the shepherd with the sheep on his shoulders, the verb keeps the initiative with the one who comes.
webster_summary: The third person singular of the present tense of come; the older form of comes. In Scripture it is often the prophetic present — what is certainly approaching spoken of as already on its way — used of Christ's advent and of the salvation that arrives from God.
webster_full: COMETH, v. [Sax. cymþ.] The third person singular of the present tense of come; contracted in modern usage to comes.
2. To move toward; to approach; to draw near; opposed to go.
3. To arrive; to happen; to come to pass; as, the day cometh.
4. In the prophetic style the present is used of the future to express certainty; as, the Son of man cometh.
5. In Scripture, from him cometh my salvation, Psa. 62; the Son of man cometh, Matt. 24.
corruption_summary: The return of Christ has been quietly moved out of the church's working expectation — treated as a doctrine held rather than an event awaited, or else sunk under charts and date-setting schemes that Scripture never authorised. The present tense restores the plain expectation.
corruption_paragraphs: Two failures crowd out watchfulness. The first is a practical unbelief that keeps the article in the creed and never lets it touch the calendar; the church confesses that Christ shall come to judge, and then plans as though He will not. Peter foretold precisely this — scoffers asking where the promise of His coming is, since all things continue as they were. The remedy is not excitement but the ordinary readiness Christ commands: a servant found doing his duty when his lord returns.

The second failure is the speculative machinery of dispensational premillennialism, a nineteenth-century system (Darby, Scofield) unknown to any Reformation confession, which divides the return into stages, times the church's removal against a calendar of tribulation, and has produced a long line of failed predictions. The dictionary's position is the historic Reformed one: a single, visible, bodily return of Christ, at an hour no man knows, to raise the dead and judge the world. The millennial question remains open within Reformed orthodoxy; the date does not, because Christ said plainly that it is not given us to know it.
roots_summary: Hebrew commonly uses the participle of bo' (to come) for imminent action; Greek erchomai in the present indicative frequently carries future reference, the futuristic present of certainty.
roots_lines: Hebrew bo' (H935) — to come in, to arrive, to enter; its participle expresses the one who is coming.
Greek erchetai (G2064) — he cometh; the present indicative of erchomai, often used of certain future events.
Greek parousia (G3952) — a presence or arrival; the technical noun for the coming of Christ.
Hebrew yeshu'ah (H3444) — salvation, deliverance; that which comes from God in Psalm 62:1.
Saxon cymþ — the Old English third singular present of cuman, to come.
usage: Of the certainty of Christ's return at an unknown hour: in such an hour as ye think not the Son of man cometh (Matthew 24:44).
Of salvation as a thing arriving from outside the self: from him cometh my salvation (Psalm 62:1).
Of the shepherd's return with the recovered sheep: when he cometh home, he calleth together his friends (Luke 15:6).
scriptures: Matthew 24:44
Therefore be ye also ready: for in such an hour as ye think not the Son of man cometh.
Psalm 62:1
To the chief Musician, to Jeduthun, A Psalm of David. Truly my soul waiteth upon God: from him cometh my salvation.
John 12:13
Took branches of palm trees, and went forth to meet him, and cried, Hosanna: Blessed is the King of Israel that cometh in the name of the Lord.
Luke 15:6
And when he cometh home, he calleth together his friends and neighbours, saying unto them, Rejoice with me; for I have found my sheep which was lost.

pos: v. (third person singular present of go; rendering Hebrew halak and yatsa', Greek hupagei and ekporeuetai)
etymology: From Saxon gæþ, the third person singular present of gan, to go. It is the older goes, and in Scripture it is frequently paired with forth to describe an army, a whirlwind, or a word issuing out from its source.
biblical_def: Goeth is the older goes, and Scripture uses it for two very different motions. The first is the settled course of a life, especially a bad one: “the hairy scalp of such an one as goeth on still in his trespasses” (Psalm 68:21). The phrase describes not a fall but a walk — sin continued in, deliberately, after warning. The second is the going forth of something sent: “When the host goeth forth against thine enemies, then keep thee from every wicked thing” (Deuteronomy 23:9), where Israel's army on campaign is put under a stricter holiness than at home, because the LORD walks in the midst of the camp. Jeremiah uses the same construction of judgment: “the whirlwind of the LORD goeth forth with fury” (Jeremiah 30:23). And the Lord names a class of affliction that yields only to a particular discipline: “this kind goeth not out but by prayer and fasting” (Matthew 17:21). The verb is plain, but where it falls it usually marks either a persistence that will be judged or a power that has been dispatched.
webster_summary: The third person singular of the present tense of go; the older form of goes. In Scripture it marks the settled course of a life continued in sin, and, with forth, the sending out of an army, a whirlwind of judgment, or a word from God.
webster_full: GOETH, v. [Sax. gæþ.] The third person singular of the present tense of go; contracted in modern usage to goes.
2. To move; to pass; to proceed from one place or state to another.
3. With forth, to issue; to be sent out; as, the word goeth forth.
4. To walk; to be habitually engaged in a course; as, he goeth on in his trespasses.
5. In Scripture, such an one as goeth on still in his trespasses, Psa. 68; this kind goeth not out but by prayer and fasting, Matt. 17.
corruption_summary: Persistent, deliberate sin is now widely reclassified as identity or as an unhealthy pattern to be managed, rather than as trespass continued in against light. Scripture's category is a man who goeth on still — a walk, chosen and repeated, for which he is answerable.
corruption_paragraphs: Therapeutic language has largely replaced moral language for habitual sin, and the replacement is not neutral. To call a besetting sin a pattern, a struggle, or a wound relocates it from the will to the circumstances, and where there is no agent there can be no repentance. Scripture is more honest and, in the end, more hopeful: it names the thing as trespass, holds the man responsible, and then offers a remedy that actually addresses guilt. A sin managed is a sin retained; a sin confessed is a sin forgiven.

The graver form of the error makes the sin an identity, so that turning from it would be a betrayal of the self. Scripture never permits that reasoning. It speaks of what men were — and such were some of you: but ye are washed — and treats the old life as something put off like a garment. Psalm 68:21 is deliberately severe because presumption is the last stage before judgment, and the man in view is not the one who stumbles but the one who has decided. The severity is mercy, since a warning is only useful while there is time to heed it.
roots_summary: Hebrew halak is to walk or go, and is the standard metaphor for the moral course of a life; yatsa' is to go out or forth, used of armies and of the word of the LORD; Greek uses hupago and ekporeuomai.
roots_lines: Hebrew halak (H1980) — to walk, to go; the standing biblical figure for the whole course of a man's life.
Hebrew yatsa' (H3318) — to go out or forth; used of the host going to war and of the word going out of God's mouth.
Hebrew 'asham (H817) and pesha' (H6588) — guilt and trespass; what the persistent man goes on in.
Greek ekporeuomai (G1607) — to go out, to proceed from; used of what issues from the heart and the mouth.
Saxon gæþ — the Old English third singular present of gan, to go.
usage: Of sin persisted in after warning: such an one as goeth on still in his trespasses (Psalm 68:21).
Of holiness required of an army in the field: When the host goeth forth against thine enemies (Deuteronomy 23:9).
Of an affliction that yields only to a particular discipline: this kind goeth not out but by prayer and fasting (Matthew 17:21).
scriptures: Psalm 68:21
But God shall wound the head of his enemies, and the hairy scalp of such an one as goeth on still in his trespasses.
Deuteronomy 23:9
When the host goeth forth against thine enemies, then keep thee from every wicked thing.
Jeremiah 30:23
Behold, the whirlwind of the LORD goeth forth with fury, a continuing whirlwind: it shall fall with pain upon the head of the wicked.
Matthew 17:21
Howbeit this kind goeth not out but by prayer and fasting.

pos: v. (third person singular present of make; rendering Hebrew 'asah and sum, Greek poiei)
etymology: From Saxon macaþ, the third person singular present of macian, to make. It is the older makes, and in Scripture it very often has God as its subject — the verb of a Creator who is still acting.
biblical_def: Maketh is the older makes, and its most striking uses put God in the subject. When Moses pleads that he is not eloquent, the LORD answers with a question that concedes nothing: “Who hath made man's mouth? or who maketh the dumb, or deaf, or the seeing, or the blind? have not I the LORD?” (Exodus 4:11). The verse is one of the plainest assertions in Scripture that God's sovereignty reaches into infirmity itself, and it is offered as a comfort to a man making excuses. The psalmist uses the same verb for the ending of wars: “He maketh wars to cease unto the end of the earth; he breaketh the bow, and cutteth the spear in sunder” (Psalm 46:9). Proverbs uses it for the ordinary operation of providence through diligence and haste: “the hand of the diligent maketh rich” (Proverbs 10:4), set against “he that maketh haste to be rich shall not be innocent” (Proverbs 28:20). The two proverbs are not in conflict; the first commends labour, the second condemns the shortcut. In each case the verb keeps something being actively made rather than merely happening.
webster_summary: The third person singular of the present tense of make; the older form of makes. In Scripture it is often the verb of God's continuing action — who maketh the dumb or deaf, who maketh wars to cease — and of the providence that attends diligence and rebukes haste.
webster_full: MAKETH, v. [Sax. macaþ.] The third person singular of the present tense of make; contracted in modern usage to makes.
2. To produce; to effect; to cause to exist; to form of materials.
3. To constitute; to appoint; to cause to be; as, he maketh the dumb.
4. To compel or cause; as, he maketh wars to cease.
5. In Scripture, who maketh the dumb, or deaf? Exo. 4; the hand of the diligent maketh rich, Prov. 10.
corruption_summary: Exodus 4:11 is the verse modern religion most wants to soften, because it says that God Himself makes the deaf and the blind. Every attempt to relieve Him of it — by limiting His power, His knowledge, or His involvement — costs more than it saves.
corruption_paragraphs: The verse is a comfort in its context and is meant to be. Moses objects that he is slow of speech; the LORD does not deny the impediment but claims it, and the claim is the ground of the promise that follows: I will be with thy mouth, and teach thee what thou shalt say. A God who merely permits infirmity can promise nothing about it. A God who makes the mouth can use it. Open theism and process theology both purchase a tidier problem of evil at the price of this comfort, and every historic Christian confession refuses the trade.

Scripture does not leave the matter as bare sovereignty. Christ, meeting a man blind from birth, is asked whose sin caused it and rejects the question outright — the blindness was that the works of God should be made manifest in him. Affliction in the hand of God is purposive, not arbitrary, and the whole book of Job stands as the extended proof that a sufferer may be denied the reason and still be answered. The Reformed doctrine of providence holds both: nothing befalls the creature outside God's ordering, and God is never the author of sin. To surrender either half is to lose the God who actually speaks in Exodus 4.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'asah is the general verb of making or doing, and sum is to set, place, or appoint; both are rendered maketh. Greek poieo covers both making and doing, and is the verb of Psalm 46:9 in the Septuagint.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'asah (H6213) — to do, to make, to fashion; the ordinary verb of divine and human production.
Hebrew sum (H7760) — to set, to appoint, to constitute; the verb behind who maketh the dumb in Exodus 4:11.
Hebrew charuts (H2742) — sharp, diligent; the quality whose hand maketh rich in Proverbs 10:4.
Greek poieo (G4160) — to make or to do; used of God's works and of man's.
Saxon macaþ — the Old English third singular present of macian, to make.
usage: Of God's sovereignty reaching into infirmity: who maketh the dumb, or deaf, or the seeing, or the blind? (Exodus 4:11).
Of God ending wars by breaking the weapons: He maketh wars to cease unto the end of the earth (Psalm 46:9).
Of diligence and haste contrasted: the hand of the diligent maketh rich (Proverbs 10:4).
scriptures: Exodus 4:11
And the LORD said unto him, Who hath made man's mouth? or who maketh the dumb, or deaf, or the seeing, or the blind? have not I the LORD?
Psalm 46:9
He maketh wars to cease unto the end of the earth; he breaketh the bow, and cutteth the spear in sunder; he burneth the chariot in the fire.
Proverbs 10:4
He becometh poor that dealeth with a slack hand: but the hand of the diligent maketh rich.
Proverbs 28:20
A faithful man shall abound with blessings: but he that maketh haste to be rich shall not be innocent.

pos: v. (second person singular of may; rendering Hebrew imperfect of permission, Greek subjunctive of purpose)
etymology: From Saxon miht, second person singular of magan, to be able or permitted. It carries two senses that English still distinguishes: permission granted (thou mayest eat) and purpose intended (that thou mayest live).
biblical_def: Mayest is the second person singular of may, and its first appearance in Scripture is a permission so wide that the prohibition following it looks small: “Of every tree of the garden thou mayest freely eat” (Genesis 2:16). The order is deliberate and is worth dwelling on. God's generosity is stated first, in the freest possible terms, and only afterward is one tree withheld. Every temptation since has worked by reversing that order, presenting the single prohibition as though it were the whole of God's dealing. The same permission governs the vineyard law: a man passing through his neighbour's vineyard “mayest eat grapes thy fill at thine own pleasure; but thou shalt not put any in thy vessel” (Deuteronomy 23:24) — hunger relieved without harvest stolen. The other sense, purpose, appears in the covenant blessings: “I will send grass in thy fields for thy cattle, that thou mayest eat and be full” (Deuteronomy 11:15), and in the psalm's account of chastening, which is given “That thou mayest give him rest from the days of adversity” (Psalm 94:13). Permission and purpose, freely given and wisely aimed.
webster_summary: The second person singular of may; used only with thou. It expresses permission granted — of every tree thou mayest freely eat — and purpose intended — that thou mayest eat and be full.
webster_full: MAYEST, v. [Sax. miht.] The second person singular of may; as, thou mayest.
2. To be permitted; to have liberty or licence; as, thou mayest go.
3. To be possible; to express purpose or end; as, that thou mayest live.
4. It is used only with thou; with ye or you the form is may.
5. In Scripture, Of every tree of the garden thou mayest freely eat, Gen. 2; that thou mayest eat and be full, Deut. 11.
corruption_summary: God is popularly imagined as a withholder whose word is chiefly a list of prohibitions. Genesis 2:16 puts the permission first and makes it nearly unlimited, and any account of God's law that begins with the restriction has already misrepresented Him.
corruption_paragraphs: The serpent's method is to quote the prohibition and suppress the permission: Yea, hath God said, Ye shall not eat of every tree of the garden? The question is a distortion by omission, since what God actually said was that Adam might freely eat of every tree but one. Eve's reply shows the damage already done, for she adds a restriction God never gave — neither shall ye touch it — and a God imagined as harsher than He is becomes easy to disobey. Every caricature of the Christian life as a system of denials repeats the same trick.

The recovery is not permissiveness but proportion. The one prohibition in Eden was real, and the death threatened was real; the law of God binds and the transgression of it is fatal. But the frame around it is the freeness of God's giving, and the same frame holds in the gospel — He that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not with him also freely give us all things? The vineyard law of Deuteronomy 23:24 shows the same generous instinct in ordinary legislation: a hungry traveller may eat his fill, and only the vessel is forbidden. God gives widely and forbids narrowly, and the man who has that order right will find obedience a very different thing.
roots_summary: Hebrew expresses permission by the imperfect, often strengthened by the infinitive absolute ('akol to'kel, thou mayest freely eat); purpose is carried by lema'an; Greek uses the subjunctive with hina.
roots_lines: Hebrew infinitive absolute — a doubled verb for emphasis; 'akol to'kel, eating thou mayest eat, rendered freely eat.
Hebrew lema'an (H4616) — to the intent that, in order that; the particle of purpose behind that thou mayest.
Greek hina (G2443) — that, in order that; with the subjunctive it expresses purpose.
Greek exesti (G1832) — it is lawful, it is permitted; the verb of permission proper.
Saxon magan — to be able or permitted; the root of both may and might.
usage: Of God's permission stated before His prohibition: Of every tree of the garden thou mayest freely eat (Genesis 2:16).
Of hunger relieved without harvest stolen: thou mayest eat grapes thy fill at thine own pleasure (Deuteronomy 23:24).
Of chastening given with a purpose: That thou mayest give him rest from the days of adversity (Psalm 94:13).
scriptures: Genesis 2:16
And the LORD God commanded the man, saying, Of every tree of the garden thou mayest freely eat:
Deuteronomy 23:24
When thou comest into thy neighbour's vineyard, then thou mayest eat grapes thy fill at thine own pleasure; but thou shalt not put any in thy vessel.
Deuteronomy 11:15
And I will send grass in thy fields for thy cattle, that thou mayest eat and be full.
Psalm 94:13
That thou mayest give him rest from the days of adversity, until the pit be digged for the wicked.

pos: v. (second person singular of should; rendering Hebrew imperfect in purpose clauses, Greek subjunctive)
etymology: The past and subjunctive of shalt, from Saxon sceoldest. Where shalt lays an obligation, shouldest states the obligation as a purpose, a duty owed, or a consequence that ought to follow — often in a clause introduced by that.
biblical_def: Shouldest is the second person singular of should, and in the Authorized Version it usually stands in a purpose or result clause: that thou shouldest. God's first commandment to man is reported in exactly that form: “whereof I commanded thee that thou shouldest not eat” (Genesis 3:11). Moses uses it to close off every excuse for ignorance of the law: the word is not beyond the sea, “that thou shouldest say, Who shall go over the sea for us” (Deuteronomy 30:13) — the commandment is near, in the mouth and in the heart, and Paul takes up the same passage to describe the nearness of the word of faith. Job uses it in astonishment that God should trouble Himself with man at all: “And that thou shouldest visit him every morning, and try him every moment?” (Job 7:18). And Christ uses it at the grave of Lazarus to bind sight to faith in the right order: “if thou wouldest believe, thou shouldest see the glory of God” (John 11:40) — believing first, and seeing after, which is the reverse of what Martha was asking for.
webster_summary: The second person singular of should; used only with thou. It states obligation, purpose, or consequence, most often in a clause of purpose — that thou shouldest not eat, that thou shouldest see the glory of God.
webster_full: SHOULDEST, v. [Sax. sceoldest.] The second person singular of should; as, thou shouldest.
2. Should is the past tense and the subjunctive of shall, and retains its primary sense of obligation.
3. It is used in clauses of purpose and consequence; as, that thou shouldest live.
4. It is used only with thou; with ye or you the form is should.
5. In Scripture, I commanded thee that thou shouldest not eat, Gen. 3; that thou shouldest see the glory of God, John 11.
corruption_summary: The order Christ gives at the grave — believe, and then see — is habitually inverted into a demand that God prove Himself first. Faith that waits for evidence before trusting is not the faith Scripture describes, and it is not the faith to which the promises are made.
corruption_paragraphs: Martha's hesitation is entirely reasonable and entirely wrong: Lord, by this time he stinketh: for he hath been dead four days. Christ's answer does not argue with the chemistry; it reasserts the order. If thou wouldest believe, thou shouldest see the glory of God. Faith is not the conclusion drawn from a miracle already witnessed but the condition on which the sight is given. This is the pattern throughout Scripture — Abraham believed and then received Isaac, Israel walked into the sea before it parted, the lepers were cleansed as they went. A demand for proof in advance is not neutral caution; it is the refusal to take God at His word.

Deuteronomy 30:13 forecloses the other evasion, which is not doubt but distance. The commandment is not in heaven nor beyond the sea, so that a man might plead that someone must fetch it for him; it is near, in his mouth and in his heart, and therefore he is without excuse. Paul quotes the passage in Romans 10 to say the same of the gospel: the word of faith which we preach is near. Between the man who says he needs more evidence and the man who says he needs more access, Scripture leaves neither a place to stand.
roots_summary: Hebrew expresses purpose and consequence by the imperfect with pen (lest) or lema'an (that); Greek uses hina with the subjunctive; English renders both by that thou shouldest.
roots_lines: Hebrew pen (H6435) — lest, that not; introduces the negative purpose clause, as in the Eden prohibition.
Hebrew lema'an (H4616) — that, to the intent that; the positive purpose particle.
Greek hina (G2443) — that, in order that; with the subjunctive, the standard purpose construction of the New Testament.
Greek doxa (G1391) — glory; what Martha was promised she should see upon believing.
Saxon sceoldest — the Old English past second singular of sceal, to owe or be obliged.
usage: Of the first commandment recalled in its purpose clause: I commanded thee that thou shouldest not eat (Genesis 3:11).
Of the nearness of God's word closing off excuse: that thou shouldest say, Who shall go over the sea for us? (Deuteronomy 30:13).
Of faith preceding sight: if thou wouldest believe, thou shouldest see the glory of God (John 11:40).
scriptures: Genesis 3:11
And he said, Who told thee that thou wast naked? Hast thou eaten of the tree, whereof I commanded thee that thou shouldest not eat?
Deuteronomy 30:13
Neither is it beyond the sea, that thou shouldest say, Who shall go over the sea for us, and bring it unto us, that we may hear it, and do it?
Job 7:18
And that thou shouldest visit him every morning, and try him every moment?
John 11:40
Jesus saith unto her, Said I not unto thee, that, if thou wouldest believe, thou shouldest see the glory of God?

pos: v. (second person singular of would; rendering Hebrew 'abah and conditional imperfects, Greek imperfect and optative)
etymology: The past and subjunctive of wilt, from Saxon woldest. It keeps the root sense of willing: what a person was willing to do, or would be willing to do, or wishes were done. Its negative — thou wouldest not — is the standing biblical description of Israel's refusal.
biblical_def: Wouldest is the second person singular of would, and it turns on the will. Its most solemn use is the indictment of a settled refusal: “ye shall be left few in number... because thou wouldest not obey the voice of the LORD thy God” (Deuteronomy 28:62). The clause names the cause of the curse and puts it in the will, not in circumstance or ignorance. It is the same construction Christ uses over Jerusalem — how often would I have gathered thy children together... and ye would not. Turned toward God in prayer, the word becomes the great cry for intervention: “Oh that thou wouldest rend the heavens, that thou wouldest come down, that the mountains might flow down at thy presence” (Isaiah 64:1). It also frames the law of mercy toward an enemy's animal: if thou see the ass of him that hateth thee lying under his burden, “and wouldest forbear to help him, thou shalt surely help with him” (Exodus 23:5) — the law anticipating exactly the unwillingness a man will feel, naming it, and overruling it. Willing and unwilling, in Scripture, are never merely private; they are the hinge of blessing and curse.
webster_summary: The second person singular of would; used only with thou. It expresses willingness, wish, or, in the negative, settled refusal — because thou wouldest not obey — and in prayer becomes the cry for God to act: Oh that thou wouldest rend the heavens.
webster_full: WOULDEST, v. [Sax. woldest.] The second person singular of would; as, thou wouldest.
2. Would is the past tense and the subjunctive of will, and retains its primary sense of volition.
3. It expresses wish or desire; as, would that it were so.
4. It is used only with thou; with ye or you the form is would.
5. In Scripture, because thou wouldest not obey the voice of the LORD thy God, Deut. 28; Oh that thou wouldest rend the heavens, Isa. 64.
corruption_summary: Unbelief is commonly explained as a want of evidence or of opportunity. Scripture locates it in the will — ye would not — and that diagnosis, unwelcome as it is, is the only one that leaves room for a remedy.
corruption_paragraphs: Christ's lament over Jerusalem puts the whole matter in three words. He had gathered, sent, warned, and wept; the city's answer was ye would not. He does not say they could not understand, nor that the evidence was thin, nor that the times were against Him. The obstacle was the will, and this is what Scripture means when it speaks of a heart of stone. The natural man is not neutral toward God and waiting for better arguments; he is unwilling, and he is responsible for his unwillingness.

The doctrine cuts both ways, which is why it is good news. If the barrier were intellectual, the remedy would be a better argument, and many are past arguing. If the barrier is the will, the remedy is regeneration — a new heart, given, not achieved — and God has promised exactly that: A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you. So Isaiah's prayer is the right one, and it is a prayer for God to do what men will not do for themselves: Oh that thou wouldest rend the heavens, that thou wouldest come down. What men would not, God can make them willing to.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'abah, to be willing, appears overwhelmingly in the negative — Israel would not; lu introduces the wish; Greek uses the imperfect of thelo for the settled refusal and ophelon for the wish.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'abah (H14) — to be willing, to consent; in the Old Testament almost always negated, of Israel's refusal.
Hebrew lu (H3863) — O that, would that; the particle of longing behind Isaiah 64:1.
Hebrew qara' (H7167) — to rend or tear; the verb of the heavens torn open in Isaiah's prayer.
Greek thelo (G2309) — to will or wish; its imperfect renders ye would not in Christ's lament.
Saxon woldest — the Old English past second singular of willan, to will.
usage: Of settled refusal named as the cause of judgment: because thou wouldest not obey the voice of the LORD thy God (Deuteronomy 28:62).
Of the prophet's cry for God to intervene: Oh that thou wouldest rend the heavens, that thou wouldest come down (Isaiah 64:1).
Of the law overruling an anticipated unwillingness: wouldest forbear to help him, thou shalt surely help with him (Exodus 23:5).
scriptures: Deuteronomy 28:62
And ye shall be left few in number, whereas ye were as the stars of heaven for multitude; because thou wouldest not obey the voice of the LORD thy God.
Isaiah 64:1
Oh that thou wouldest rend the heavens, that thou wouldest come down, that the mountains might flow down at thy presence,
Exodus 23:5
If thou see the ass of him that hateth thee lying under his burden, and wouldest forbear to help him, thou shalt surely help with him.
1 Kings 18:9
And he said, What have I sinned, that thou wouldest deliver thy servant into the hand of Ahab, to slay me?

pos: v. (second person singular of could; rendering Hebrew and Greek expressions of ability)
etymology: The past of canst, from Saxon cuþest, second person singular of cunnan, to be able or to know how. It occurs five times in the Authorized Version, and each occurrence turns on what a person was, or was not, able to do.
biblical_def: Couldest is the second person singular of could, and its five occurrences in Scripture are unusually weighty. The greatest is Christ's answer to Pilate, who had just claimed the power of life and death: “Thou couldest have no power at all against me, except it were given thee from above” (John 19:11). The Roman governor is not told that his authority is unreal but that it is derived, and the whole biblical doctrine of the civil magistrate is contained in that clause. Christ stands bound before a man who genuinely holds the sword, and He grounds that man's power in the throne of God. Daniel receives similar words from a pagan king who at least sees where the ability came from: “seeing thou couldest reveal this secret” (Daniel 2:47). In Gethsemane the word is a reproach so gentle it wounds: “Simon, sleepest thou? couldest not thou watch one hour?” (Mark 14:37). And Jeremiah uses it of a nation that spent its whole capacity on evil: “thou hast spoken and done evil things as thou couldest” (Jeremiah 3:5).
webster_summary: The second person singular of could, the past of canst; used only with thou. It occurs five times in Scripture, most weightily in Christ's word to Pilate that no power could be held against Him except it were given from above.
webster_full: COULDEST, v. [Sax. cuþest.] The second person singular of could, the past tense of can; as, thou couldest.
2. Can, from Sax. cunnan, signifies to be able, and also to know how.
3. It expresses ability, power, or capacity, whether physical, moral or official.
4. It is used only with thou; with ye or you the form is could.
5. In Scripture, Thou couldest have no power at all against me, John 19; couldest not thou watch one hour? Mark 14.
corruption_summary: Political authority is treated either as absolute in itself or as a mere social arrangement with no divine warrant. Christ's word to Pilate refuses both: the magistrate's power is real, and it is entirely derived from God, and therefore accountable to Him.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors divide the modern field. The first makes the state the highest authority, answerable to nothing above itself, so that whatever it legislates is by definition lawful; against this stands the plain fact that Pilate's power was given, and what is given is held on terms. The second treats government as a purely human convention with no divine institution behind it, which leaves obedience without ground and resistance without limit. Scripture teaches that the powers that be are ordained of God, that the magistrate is God's minister for good, and that he will answer for the sword he bears.

The dictionary holds the classical two-kingdoms position of the Reformers, in which family, church, and state are each God-ordained with a proper sphere, and Christ is Lord over all of them. Radical Two-Kingdoms theology, by contrast, tries to release the civil realm from Christ's lordship altogether and govern it by natural law alone; Christ's answer in the judgment hall will not permit that division, since He asserts His authority over Pilate's office while standing in Pilate's custody. The same verse also fixes the limit of the magistrate's guilt and of the guilt of those who delivered Christ to him — therefore he that delivered me unto thee hath the greater sin — which is a warning to every man who uses lawful power for unlawful ends.
roots_summary: Hebrew expresses ability by yakol, to be able or to prevail; Greek by dunamai, to have power, from which comes dunamis, power itself; the Saxon root cunnan means both to be able and to know how.
roots_lines: Hebrew yakol (H3201) — to be able, to prevail, to endure; the ordinary verb of capacity.
Greek dunamai (G1410) — to be able, to have power; the verb behind thou couldest have no power.
Greek exousia (G1849) — authority, right, delegated power; the noun Pilate claimed and Christ traced to its source.
Greek anothen (G509) — from above, from the beginning; the source of Pilate's authority in John 19:11.
Saxon cunnan — to be able and to know how; the root of can, could, and cunning.
usage: Of the civil magistrate's derived authority: Thou couldest have no power at all against me, except it were given thee from above (John 19:11).
Of a pagan king acknowledging the source of Daniel's gift: seeing thou couldest reveal this secret (Daniel 2:47).
Of a gentle reproach in Gethsemane: couldest not thou watch one hour? (Mark 14:37).
scriptures: John 19:11
Jesus answered, Thou couldest have no power at all against me, except it were given thee from above: therefore he that delivered me unto thee hath the greater sin.
Daniel 2:47
The king answered unto Daniel, and said, Of a truth it is, that your God is a God of gods, and a Lord of kings, and a revealer of secrets, seeing thou couldest reveal this secret.
Mark 14:37
And he cometh, and findeth them sleeping, and saith unto Peter, Simon, sleepest thou? couldest not thou watch one hour?
Jeremiah 3:5
Will he reserve his anger for ever? will he keep it to the end? Behold, thou hast spoken and done evil things as thou couldest.

pos: v. (third person singular present of sit; rendering Hebrew yashab, Greek kathetai)
etymology: From Saxon siteþ, the third person singular present of sittan. Hebrew yashab means both to sit and to dwell or be enthroned, and it is this royal sense that dominates the biblical use: to sit is to reign, to judge, and to remain.
biblical_def: Sitteth is the older sits, and in Scripture sitting is very often reigning. “The LORD sitteth upon the flood; yea, the LORD sitteth King for ever” (Psalm 29:10) sets God enthroned above the very waters that overwhelmed the world, which is the psalm's answer to every storm it has been describing. Sitting is also judging: “A king that sitteth in the throne of judgment scattereth away all evil with his eyes” (Proverbs 20:8), and the accession of Solomon is reported in the same posture — “Solomon sitteth on the throne of the kingdom” (1 Kings 1:46). Against this royal background Christ's question at the last supper is deliberately jarring: “whether is greater, he that sitteth at meat, or he that serveth? is not he that sitteth at meat? but I am among you as he that serveth” (Luke 22:27). The One who sits at the right hand of the Majesty on high took the servant's place at the table. And Lamentations gives the posture its other meaning, endurance under affliction: “He sitteth alone and keepeth silence, because he hath borne it upon him” (Lamentations 3:28).
webster_summary: The third person singular of the present tense of sit; the older form of sits. In Scripture sitting is chiefly enthronement and judgment — the LORD sitteth King for ever — and also the posture of endurance under affliction.
webster_full: SITTETH, v. [Sax. siteþ.] The third person singular of the present tense of sit; contracted in modern usage to sits.
2. To rest upon the lower extremity of the body; to be seated.
3. To be placed on a throne or seat of judgment; to reign; to judge.
4. To remain; to abide; to dwell; answering to the Hebrew yashab.
5. In Scripture, the LORD sitteth King for ever, Psa. 29; he that sitteth at meat, Luke 22.
corruption_summary: The session of Christ — His sitting at the Father's right hand — is among the most neglected articles of the creed, though it is the church's guarantee that the work of atonement is finished and that a Man now reigns over history.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle needing recovery is the present session of Christ. The Old Testament priests stood daily at their service, because their work was never done; the epistle to the Hebrews makes the contrast the whole point — this man, after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down on the right hand of God. The sitting is the proof of the finishing. A church that neglects the session tends to preach an atonement still somehow in progress, and to live as though the outcome of history were undecided.

The session also settles the question of who governs. He is seated far above all principality, and power, and might, and dominion, and the same passage says He was given to be head over all things to the church. This is the ground of Christian courage in a hostile age: not that circumstances are favourable, but that the throne is occupied. And Luke 22:27 keeps the doctrine from breeding arrogance in His servants, for the One who sits enthroned is the One who took the towel. Authority in Christ's kingdom is exercised in the shape of His own.
roots_summary: Hebrew yashab covers sitting, dwelling, remaining, and being enthroned; kisse' is the throne itself. Greek kathemai is to sit, and kathizo to seat oneself, the verb of Christ's session in Hebrews.
roots_lines: Hebrew yashab (H3427) — to sit, dwell, remain, be enthroned; the single verb behind all these senses.
Hebrew kisse' (H3678) — a throne or seat of honour; the place of both royal rule and judgment.
Greek kathemai (G2521) — to sit, to be seated; used of the Lamb and of Him that sat upon the throne.
Greek kathizo (G2523) — to sit down; the aorist in Hebrews 10:12 marks the finished sacrifice.
Greek diakoneo (G1247) — to serve or minister; set against sitting at meat in Luke 22:27.
usage: Of God enthroned above the waters of the flood: the LORD sitteth King for ever (Psalm 29:10).
Of a king in the seat of judgment: A king that sitteth in the throne of judgment scattereth away all evil with his eyes (Proverbs 20:8).
Of Christ taking the servant's place at the table: is not he that sitteth at meat? but I am among you as he that serveth (Luke 22:27).
scriptures: Psalm 29:10
The LORD sitteth upon the flood; yea, the LORD sitteth King for ever.
Proverbs 20:8
A king that sitteth in the throne of judgment scattereth away all evil with his eyes.
Luke 22:27
For whether is greater, he that sitteth at meat, or he that serveth? is not he that sitteth at meat? but I am among you as he that serveth.
Lamentations 3:28
He sitteth alone and keepeth silence, because he hath borne it upon him.

pos: v. (third person singular present of ask; rendering Hebrew sha'al, Greek aitei)
etymology: From Saxon asciaþ, the third person singular present of ascian, to ask. In the Gospels it stands in two great sayings — the promise that every one who asks receives, and the command to give to him that asks — which together bind prayer and almsgiving to the same verb.
biblical_def: Asketh is the older asks, and Christ uses it twice in ways that belong together. The first is the promise: “For every one that asketh receiveth; and he that seeketh findeth; and to him that knocketh it shall be opened” (Matthew 7:8, repeated at Luke 11:10). The tense is continuous — the one who keeps asking — and the promise is universal within the family it addresses, since the following verses reason from what earthly fathers give their children to what the heavenly Father gives to them that ask Him. The second is the command that mirrors it: “Give to him that asketh thee, and from him that would borrow of thee turn not thou away” (Matthew 5:42), and again, “Give to every man that asketh of thee” (Luke 6:30). Having been heard, the disciple must hear; having received freely, he gives freely. The word appears once more with a sad edge, when the Lord notes that His disciples, absorbed in their own grief, had stopped enquiring where He was going: “none of you asketh me, Whither goest thou?” (John 16:5).
webster_summary: The third person singular of the present tense of ask; the older form of asks. In Scripture it carries Christ's promise that every one who asks receives, and His command to give to him that asks — the same verb governing prayer and almsgiving.
webster_full: ASKETH, v. [Sax. asciaþ.] The third person singular of the present tense of ask; contracted in modern usage to asks.
2. To request; to seek to obtain by words; to petition.
3. To inquire; to put a question with a view to information.
4. To require, demand or claim; as, the work asketh time.
5. In Scripture, every one that asketh receiveth, Matt. 7; Give to him that asketh thee, Matt. 5.
corruption_summary: The promise that every one who asks receives has been turned into a guarantee of whatever is asked for — health, wealth, and success on demand. Christ's own context supplies the correction: the Father gives good things, and the best of them is the Holy Spirit.
corruption_paragraphs: The prosperity gospel treats Matthew 7:8 as a mechanism: the right words, the right confidence, and the desired object must follow. But the Lord's illustration governs the promise. A father asked for bread does not give a stone, and asked for a fish does not give a serpent — and Luke's parallel names the crowning gift as the Holy Spirit. A father who gave a child everything it named would be no father at all; the promise is that God gives good, not that He gives whatever is wanted. James adds the missing clause explicitly: ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss, that ye may consume it upon your lusts.

The command in Matthew 5:42 is corrupted from the other direction, by a sentimentality that gives without discernment and by a hardness that will not give at all. Scripture holds generosity and wisdom together: the same canon that says give to him that asketh thee also says that a man who will not work shall not eat, and requires that the church's support be ordered rather than indiscriminate. The point of the command is that the disciple's default is open-handed, since he has received everything he has; the point of the wisdom literature is that open-handedness is not the same as being easily used.
roots_summary: Hebrew sha'al is to ask, request, or enquire, and gives the name Saul; Greek distinguishes aiteo, to ask as an inferior of a superior, from erotao, to ask on equal footing — a distinction the Lord observes of His own praying.
roots_lines: Hebrew sha'al (H7592) — to ask, request, enquire; the root of the name Saul, asked for.
Greek aiteo (G154) — to ask, to beg; the petition of a lesser to a greater, used of our praying.
Greek erotao (G2065) — to ask, to request; used of Christ's asking of the Father, on equal terms.
Greek lambano (G2983) — to receive, to take; the answering verb in every one that asketh receiveth.
Saxon ascian — to ask, to seek by words; the root of the English verb.
usage: Of the promise attached to persistent prayer: For every one that asketh receiveth (Matthew 7:8).
Of open-handedness commanded of the disciple: Give to him that asketh thee (Matthew 5:42).
Of disciples too absorbed in grief to enquire: none of you asketh me, Whither goest thou? (John 16:5).
scriptures: Matthew 7:8
For every one that asketh receiveth; and he that seeketh findeth; and to him that knocketh it shall be opened.
Matthew 5:42
Give to him that asketh thee, and from him that would borrow of thee turn not thou away.
Luke 6:30
Give to every man that asketh of thee; and of him that taketh away thy goods ask them not again.
John 16:5
But now I go my way to him that sent me; and none of you asketh me, Whither goest thou?
